r: This course builds the foundational literacy-methods knowledge Colorado licensure requires: phonological and phonemic awareness, the alphabetic principle, decoding, fluency, and assessment techniques for emergent K-3 readers. The applied work maps to Training and Teaching Others and Assessing the Quality of Information, and Colorado's READ Act ties elementary licensure to demonstrated evidence-based reading-instruction competency, an accreditor-approved, course-specific mandate that a program cannot substitute away. Task-exposure research finds science and critical-thinking skills negatively associated with automation exposure while observed-usage data shows writing tasks prominent, a mixed signal here since phonics content generation is drafting-adjacent but diagnosing an individual child's decoding gaps is judgment-heavy. As the prerequisite substrate for the entire literacy sequence, this course anchors five downstream required courses. At 24 months capability has not displaced the licensure requirement or the diagnostic judgment it certifies; the instrumental need remains intact and the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI tools will more competently draft phonics lesson plans, generate leveled text, and summarize literacy-development frameworks, meaningfully augmenting how candidates prepare instructional materials. But applying that knowledge to a specific emerging reader's error patterns carries a real verification burden, since a misjudged instructional strategy can entrench reading difficulty in ways that are not obvious until much later, and Colorado's READ Act licensure requirement operates on a legislative and accreditation timeline that does not turn over within a five-year window. The course also remains the prerequisite root for the rest of the literacy-methods sequence, so displacing it would require restructuring the entire program pathway. Diffusion data shows AI adoption still uneven across firms and sectors, and teacher-preparation programs are conservative adopters. The instrumental case erodes on the content-generation margin but the rating holds Low, protected by licensure and foundational role together.

Over a decade, AI capability trend data (task-time-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months) points toward far more competent, personalized literacy-instruction support, and it becomes plausible that much of the explanatory and lesson-design content this course teaches is generated at expert level. That erosion is real enough that the institutional cap loosens: a hard licensure mandate ordinarily fixes the course at Low, but ten years is enough time for accreditors or the state board to revise how reading-competency is demonstrated, so the ceiling rises to Medium rather than staying pinned at Low. Genuine uncertainty remains about whether diagnostic judgment for individual struggling readers is fully automatable or whether verification burden keeps a trained teacher essential; this is not a confident forecast of full erosion. The rating moves to Medium, reflecting capability growth against a licensure clock that only loosens at this longer horizon.
RDG 3111.d: This K-3 literacy course focuses on language arts components of emergent literacy development, including oral language development, listening, phonological and phonemic awareness, the alphabetic principle, high frequency vocabulary development, decoding, spelling, and writing development, and fluency development. Instructional strategies and assessment techniques that support the acquisition of literacy, current approaches in teaching emergent readers, and materials used in literacy instruction are also covered.

r: This course teaches K-6 writing instruction aligned to Colorado Academic Standards and the CDE Framework for Writing Instruction, covering the writing process, grammar, and spelling, with candidates explicitly applying methods "both in class and in the co-requisite literacy field" alongside the concurrent RDG 3335 placement. The applied tasks map to Training and Teaching Others and Documenting and Recording Information, and observed-usage data shows writing assistance is among the most common AI use cases, making the drafting-support content here plausibly exposed. But the course is embedded in Colorado's licensure-gated literacy block and paired with real classroom application with actual children, a course-specific mandate combined with concurrent field practice that a generative tool cannot substitute. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this evidence-based instructional competence under supervision is untouched; the rating is Low, anchored by licensure and the concurrent field requirement.

By 2031, AI will draft model writing-instruction sequences, generate mentor texts, and provide grammar and spelling feedback with real fluency, automating much of the content-preparation side of this course. Productivity research on professional writing shows large quality and speed gains from AI assistance, suggesting the drafting-support layer erodes meaningfully. Yet the course's core competence is applying evidence-based writing pedagogy to real elementary students in the co-requisite field placement, where judgment about a child's developing writing and appropriate scaffolding carries a verification burden AI does not resolve, and Colorado's licensure architecture for the K-6 literacy block does not relax on a five-year cycle. The instrumental case is dented on the planning-and-drafting margin but the applied, supervised teaching competence remains required. The rating holds Low, with the erosion concentrated in tasks adjacent to, not central to, what candidates are certified to do.

A decade of sustained capability growth, consistent with the capability trend of task-time-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months, plausibly yields AI systems that competently model, sequence, and even adaptively personalize writing instruction content, substantially eroding the content-generation rationale for this course. Because the binding constraint is a hard licensure mandate rather than a diffuse accreditation credit-hour floor, the rating would ordinarily stay pinned at Low, but a ten-year horizon is long enough that the state's approved curriculum requirements could plausibly be revised, so the ceiling loosens to Medium. Whether it actually reaches that ceiling depends on how much of the supervised, field-embedded application of writing pedagogy to real children still requires a human's judgment, which is genuinely uncertain this far out. This is a hedged forecast, not a confident prediction of automation; the rating moves to Medium, reflecting capability outrunning institutional change while stopping short of full erosion given the field-application core.
RDG 3222.d: This course focuses on K-6 writing instruction, as informed by the Colorado Academic Standards and the Colorado Department of Education Framework for Writing Instruction. Course topics include evidence-based methods for teaching components of the writing process as well as grammar and spelling. Teacher candidates experience and apply instructional methods both in class and in the co-requisite literacy field.

r: This course prepares K-12 and secondary licensure candidates to embed literacy strategies, reading, writing, speaking, viewing, and listening, into their own content-area instruction, teaching them to select scaffolds and assessment techniques for diverse learners rather than to teach early reading itself. The applied work maps to Training and Teaching Others and Developing Objectives and Strategies, since candidates learn to design content-specific literacy scaffolds, vocabulary strategies, text-structure instruction, formative literacy assessment, for subjects ranging from music to health and PE to core content areas. Task-exposure research finds writing and strategy-drafting tasks positively associated with automation exposure, and AI already drafts serviceable literacy-scaffolding activities. Still, the course sits inside Colorado's licensure requirement that content-area teachers demonstrate literacy-instruction competency, a program-level mandate layered onto each specialty program's own methods sequence. At 24 months, adoption of AI strategy-generation tools inside teacher-prep methods courses remains limited, and the licensure requirement is untouched; the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI will likely draft competent content-literacy strategy sets, generate leveled text and vocabulary scaffolds tailored to a given subject, and suggest formative-assessment items, since this content resembles the writing and lesson-preparation tasks where productivity research shows meaningful time and quality gains from AI assistance. That erodes the course's strategy-generation layer. But applying those scaffolds to actual diverse learners, English learners, students with IEPs, or students behind grade level in a specific content class, still requires professional judgment candidates are only beginning to develop, and Colorado's licensure architecture requiring demonstrated content-literacy competency across specialty programs does not loosen within a five-year window. The course's shared prerequisite structure across multiple licensure tracks, music, health and PE, and core content, also signals institutional weight beyond a single program. The instrumental case erodes on the planning margin while the program-mandate protection holds; the rating rises to Medium.

A decade of capability growth, consistent with the trend of task-time-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months, plausibly yields AI systems that generate highly tailored content-literacy scaffolds and assessment strategies for nearly any subject and learner profile, substantially eroding the course's core planning content. Because the binding constraint is a program-level licensure mandate rather than a hard, course-specific clinical requirement, the F4 ceiling loosens over a ten-year horizon, consistent with how looser program mandates are treated elsewhere in this catalog. Whether Colorado's content-literacy competency requirement is satisfied through a differently structured course, or whether candidates still need supervised practice applying scaffolds to real diverse learners, is genuinely uncertain this far out. This is a hedged forecast, not a confident prediction of removal. The rating holds Medium, reflecting capability plausibly outrunning the licensure requirement's current course-level implementation while institutional change itself remains unresolved.
RDG 3280.d: This course is for students seeking educational licensure in a K-12 or Secondary content area. Course content and objectives prepare teacher candidates to develop students' ability in reading, writing, speaking, viewing, and listening. Teacher candidates acquire literacy tools, including assessment strategies, to scaffold content instruction for diverse learners. Literacy strategies are applied to positively impact student content learning.

r: This course addresses literacy instruction for grades 4-6: comprehension expansion, vocabulary knowledge, content-area literacy, and matching assessed student abilities to instructional models, taken concurrently with the RDG 3335 field placement. The applied tasks map to Assessing the Quality of Information and Training and Teaching Others, since candidates must interpret assessment data about specific intermediate-grade readers and select instructional models accordingly. Task-exposure research finds science and critical-thinking skills negatively associated with automation exposure, and matching diagnostic data to an individual student's needs is exactly this kind of judgment-heavy work. The binding constraint is Colorado's licensure-gated literacy-methods block combined with the concurrent field experience, where real students are involved. At 24 months neither AI capability nor adoption has touched the licensure requirement or the supervised diagnostic-instructional judgment this course builds; the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI-assisted analytics could plausibly help candidates summarize comprehension and vocabulary assessment data faster, and observed-usage data shows the Computer and Mathematical category dominating current AI use, suggesting data-summarization support becomes routine. But translating that data into an appropriate instructional model for a specific 4-6 grade reader remains a judgment call with real consequences if misapplied, and the jagged-frontier research on AI use outside its competence zone warns that misplaced trust in automated recommendations can reduce accuracy rather than improve it. Colorado's licensure architecture for the literacy-methods sequence, and the course's role as prerequisite substrate for the capstone trio, do not loosen within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case for the diagnostic-application core is preserved even as data-processing assistance grows; the rating holds Low.

Ten years of capability growth, at the pace implied by task-time-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months, makes it plausible that AI handles most of the data-synthesis and instructional-model-matching content this course currently teaches through direct practice. Because the licensure mandate is the binding constraint rather than a looser accreditation credit floor, the rating's ceiling stays low longer than a typical program-mandate course, but a decade is enough time for the state's approved-curriculum requirements to plausibly shift, so the ceiling loosens to Medium. Whether the supervised, field-embedded diagnostic judgment with real intermediate-grade readers is actually displaced by then is genuinely unclear, and this is not a confident point-prediction. The rating moves to Medium, reflecting the same licensure-clock pattern seen across the literacy-methods sequence, capability ahead of institutional change but not fully substituting for the human judgment involved.
RDG 3333.d: This course focuses on literacy instruction for the intermediate grades 4-6. This course addresses several key areas: intermediate identities and literacies, effective reading and learning practices, expanding comprehension, teacher and student assessment of literacy development, learning strategies, vocabulary knowledge, and literacy in the content areas. An additional focus is matching assessed student abilities and needs to appropriate instructional models and curricular content.

r: This one-credit course requires 45 hours of direct placement in an elementary classroom, where candidates apply reading and writing knowledge to observe, plan, and practice instruction across content areas with real children under supervision. The applied work is in-person instructional practice and real-time interpersonal judgment with minors, squarely in the low-exposure, high-presence categories that task-exposure research associates with manual and physical work rather than automatable tasks. The binding constraint is absolute: Colorado educator licensure requires accumulated, logged field hours in an approved program, and no AI system can accrue or substitute for that clock-hour requirement. This mirrors the field-experience pattern seen elsewhere in teacher preparation, where the instrumental need for supervised placement is untouched by capability. At 24 months, adoption and capability are simply not the operative variables; the rating is Low with high confidence.

By 2031, AI tools will likely assist cooperating teachers and candidates with lesson planning, assessment-item generation, and data organization inside the placement classroom, changing what candidates do while in the room. But the course exists specifically to accumulate supervised, embodied clock hours managing real elementary students, a formative and presence-dependent requirement that no automation performs on the candidate's behalf. Child-welfare stakes keep verification burden high, and Colorado's field-hour mandate operates on a legislative and accreditation cycle well beyond five years. Diffusion research shows AI adoption remains uneven even where capability exists, reinforcing that classroom-level assistance will be partial and supervised. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and institutional lock-in together; AI reshapes the tools candidates use in the field, not whether the field hours must be logged in person. The rating holds Low.

Even under a decade of substantial capability growth and broader classroom AI adoption, the requirement that candidates accumulate supervised, in-person field hours with children remains among the most durable constraints in Colorado's teacher-licensure architecture, comparable to the roughly 800 secondary field hours anchoring the broader teacher-preparation pathway. The embodied, real-time, interpersonal nature of instructional practice with elementary students resists direct substitution regardless of how capable ambient or planning-assistance tools become, consistent with task-exposure research classifying manual and physical, presence-dependent work as low-exposure even as adjacent categories climb. Genuine uncertainty exists about how heavily AI mediates the instruction candidates observe and practice, but the clock-hour requirement itself, and the supervised competence it certifies, is not plausibly removed by 2036 in a central-case scenario. The rating holds Low with high confidence, the field-placement anchor of this literacy-licensure sequence remaining the most protected course in the set across all three horizons.
RDG 3335.d: This field placement involves 45 hours in an elementary school classroom. Teacher candidates apply knowledge of reading and writing development to observe and practice organizing a comprehensive plan of instruction throughout the content areas based on assessment of student abilities, appropriate instructional methods and required curriculum. Students apply a growing repertoire of various instructional models that range from general classroom structure to explicit skill teaching. This course is a field experience taken concurrently with RDG 3222 and RDG 3333.

r: This course expands candidates' conception of literacy beyond decoding and comprehension into digital literacies, disciplinary literacy, visual literacy, out-of-school literacies, and translanguaging, examining teacher and learner roles from global perspectives. Unlike the field-embedded courses in this sequence, its description names no clinical hours; the applied work is discursive and conceptual, mapping to Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others and Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge. That content is closer to the writing and synthesis tasks task-exposure research classifies as positively associated with automation exposure, since AI competently discusses digital-literacy frameworks and generates comparative perspectives on literacy theory. The course remains a required component of the literacy-licensure sequence, a program-level mandate rather than a named board-tested skill, which provides real but softer protection than the field-hour courses. At 24 months realized diffusion is still limited, so the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI will competently synthesize and even generate original discussion of digital, disciplinary, and out-of-school literacies, since this content resembles the writing and conceptual-synthesis tasks where productivity research shows large quality and time gains from AI assistance. The course's protection comes from its place inside the required literacy-preparation sequence rather than from embodiment or a hard clinical mandate, and program-level requirements of this kind do not force the exact-course structure to persist the way a named licensure exam does. With no strong foundational dependency capping the course either, since no later required course in the catalog lists it as a prerequisite, the rating rises to Medium: the conceptual content is substantially AI-generable even as candidates remain formally required to take the course under current program design.

Ten years out, AI plausibly produces literacy-theory synthesis and multi-perspective analysis of comparable quality to what this course develops, consistent with the capability trajectory implied by task-time-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months. The program-level mandate is a softer, contributory-style protection than a hard clinical requirement, and it is genuinely uncertain whether a decade of curriculum revision preserves this specific course's current design once its conceptual content is broadly AI-generable. Some protection persists in developing candidates' own professional judgment and identity around competing literacy frameworks, a reflective task less cleanly captured by output-matching benchmarks like GDPval. This is a hedged forecast rather than a confident prediction of removal. The rating holds Medium, reflecting substantial content-level exposure only partially offset by the course's continued formal place in the licensure-preparation sequence.
RDG 4222.d: This course focuses on expanding traditional definitions and conceptions of literacy in order to teach to the evolving needs of diverse populations. Expanded notions of literacy include: Digital literacies, disciplinary literacy, visual literacy, out-of-school literacies, and translanguaging. This course is intended to challenge the scope of teacher candidates' literacy knowledge and perceptions for the purpose of establishing a positive and broadened perspective of teaching and learning with expanding best practices. Teacher candidates examine the various roles of teachers, learners and literacy from global perspectives in order to further develop their teaching identities.

r: This course places candidates one-on-one with a real K-6 student in a field setting to collect, interpret, and act on individualized literacy-assessment data through a teach-assess-adjust cycle, working collaboratively with peers and other professionals. The applied work is embodied, real-time, one-to-one instructional judgment with a specific child, mapping to Assisting and Caring for Others and Assessing the Quality of Information, categories task-exposure research associates with low automation exposure given their reliance on in-person, non-obvious diagnostic judgment. The binding constraint combines Colorado's literacy-licensure mandate with genuine field-based practice with a real learner, a course-specific requirement no AI system can fulfill on the candidate's behalf. Misjudging a single child's literacy needs based on assessment data carries a real, hard-to-detect error cost. At 24 months the instrumental need for this supervised, individualized field competence is fully intact; the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI-assisted diagnostic tools may help candidates score assessments or flag patterns in a student's reading errors faster, and observed-usage data shows AI increasingly used for analytical and diagnostic-style tasks. But translating those patterns into an individualized instructional plan for one real child remains squarely inside the teach-assess-adjust cycle this course builds, and the jagged-frontier research cautions that automated suggestions used outside a practitioner's genuine expertise can degrade rather than improve accuracy, raising the verification stakes when a novice candidate is the one applying the tool. Colorado's licensure requirement for demonstrated literacy-assessment competency, tied to field-based one-on-one practice, does not relax on a five-year timeline. The rating holds Low: the embodied, individualized diagnostic-instructional core, not the mechanics of scoring, is what the course certifies and what remains protected.

A decade of capability growth plausibly makes AI diagnostic support for reading-error pattern analysis highly competent, per the task-time-horizon doubling trend, but the course's central competence is a real-time, embodied, one-on-one relationship with an individual struggling reader, work that stays inside low-exposure, high-presence categories even as adjacent analytical tasks automate. Because the licensure mandate here is course-specific and field-based rather than a looser credit-hour floor, and because no clear ten-year path exists for removing individualized supervised practice from literacy-endorsement preparation, the rating stays capped at Low rather than loosening to Medium the way looser program-mandate courses do. Some uncertainty remains about how thoroughly diagnostic scoring automates and whether that reshapes the course's emphasis, but the embodied one-on-one instructional core is not plausibly displaced by 2036. The rating holds Low with high confidence.
RDG 4333.d: In this course, the focus is on working one-on-one with a K-6 student in a field setting to collect, examine, and interpret that student's assessment data in order to provide data-based instruction in conjunction with standards. Working with one student to practice giving assessments, planning, and delivering literacy instruction based on student strengths and weaknesses provides the opportunity for an in-depth understanding of the teach-assess-adjust cycle. Collaborative work with peers and other professionals assists with skill development in aligning assessment data and literacy instruction with content.

r: This capstone course teaches candidates to collect and interpret whole-class literacy assessment data to plan instruction, covering how state and federal legislation shapes literacy instruction, differentiation methods, and collaborative team planning, with its content explicitly applied "in the partnering residency" alongside coreq student-teaching courses. The applied work maps to Analyzing Data or Information and Coordinating the Work of Others, and observed-usage data shows the Computer and Mathematical category dominates current AI use, suggesting the data-aggregation layer here is meaningfully exposed. But the course sits inside Colorado's licensure-gated literacy sequence and is directly tied to the residency placement, where real embodied classroom application with actual students occurs concurrently, a course-specific mandate that combines with real-time field practice. At 24 months the instrumental need for this supervised, residency-embedded competence is intact; the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI-assisted dashboards will likely aggregate and visualize whole-class assessment data with real competence, consistent with productivity research showing substantial gains on data-heavy analytical tasks, meaningfully automating the reporting layer of what this course teaches. But interpreting that data to plan differentiated instruction for an actual class of students, within the accountability constraints of state and federal legislation, and while embedded concurrently in the residency placement, still carries a real verification burden and requires physical presence in the room with the class being assessed. Colorado's licensure architecture for the capstone literacy sequence, tied directly to the student-teaching residency, does not relax on a five-year cycle. The instrumental case erodes on the data-aggregation margin but the applied, residency-embedded planning judgment, exercised with real students and real accountability stakes, remains required; the rating holds Low.

Over a decade, AI capability growth at the pace implied by task-time-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months plausibly yields highly competent automated data-aggregation and even differentiation-suggestion tools for whole-class literacy assessment, substantially eroding the analytical core this course teaches. Because the binding constraint is a hard, residency-tied licensure mandate, the rating would ordinarily stay at Low, but ten years is enough time for Colorado's approved-curriculum requirements to plausibly be revised, loosening the ceiling to Medium. Whether the course actually reaches that ceiling depends on how much of the accountability-and-planning judgment embedded in real residency practice with actual students still needs a human, which remains genuinely uncertain this far out. The rating moves to Medium, reflecting capability outrunning institutional change while the residency-embedded application keeps it from rating higher.
RDG 4444.d: This course focuses on collecting and interpreting whole class assessment data in order to plan literacy instruction. Topics include how state and federal legislation affect literacy instruction, as well as methods for differentiating literacy instruction. Collaborative planning as part of an educational team is a further focus. Application of this course content will be in the partnering residency.

r: This course gives psychology majors and minors intensive experience as an undergraduate teaching assistant under close faculty supervision, combining seminar meetings with weekly hours of application: preparing a learning environment, selecting textbooks, writing instructional materials, and receiving guidance on job and graduate-school preparation. Unlike the RDG literacy-licensure courses, this is not accreditation- or licensure-gated; its general-studies field is empty and no other course lists it as a prerequisite, so no strong institutional lock-in protects it. The applied work maps to Training and Teaching Others and Coaching and Developing Others, and includes real in-person facilitation with students, an embodied, presence-dependent activity distinct from the material-preparation and writing tasks observed-usage data shows AI already assists with well. At 24 months, close faculty supervision and the live TA role keep the instrumental case for hands-on experience largely intact; the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI will competently draft syllabi content, suggest textbook selections, and generate instructional materials, automating much of the preparation-side work this course teaches, consistent with productivity research showing large gains on professional writing and drafting tasks. That leaves the embodied, real-time TA role, facilitating discussion, supporting learners directly in the classroom, and receiving mentorship toward graduate school or employment, which remains presence-dependent and only modestly exposed to current automation. With no licensure mandate or foundational role protecting the course, and its material-preparation content substantially AI-generable, the rating rises to Medium: content-preparation assistance meaningfully changes what the TA role involves even as the live facilitation and close faculty-mentoring component keeps full automation of the assistantship from being realized within this five-year window.

A decade out, AI plausibly handles the large majority of course-preparation work, material selection, and even drafting feedback for students, given the capability trajectory implied by task-time-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months, and this course carries no licensure, accreditation, or foundational-role constraint to hold the rating down. What remains is the embodied mentoring and live facilitation experience, real value for a candidate's own development, but a narrower slice of the course's original content than the full preparation-and-instruction curriculum it currently covers. The uncertainty here is genuine: whether faculty-supervised TA roles persist in their current form or shrink toward pure mentorship is unclear this far out. The rating holds Medium, reflecting substantial content-level exposure balanced against the embodied facilitation core that AI does not perform for the candidate.
RDG 4970.d: This course provides intensive experience as an undergraduate teaching assistant under close faculty supervision. The experience includes lecture/seminar meetings and additional hours of application each week. During the seminar portion of the course, students will learn about preparing a learning environment, performing textbook selection, and writing materials required for teaching. Students will also be given guidance on job/graduate school preparation.
